43rd1st:Bill 4.purpose: Updates BC's consumer-protection law to modernize the rules for consumer contracts. It sets transparency requirements for contracts and targets contract terms that restrict people's access to justice, with the aim of keeping costs down and helping people avoid fraud. Sponsored by Attorney General Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 4.vote_analysis: He voted yea on second reading, which passed unanimously, 91–0, on March 3, 2025, so the bill's principle had every voting member's support. He did not speak on the bill, so his own reasons are not on the record. What the votes show is support for the bill with changes: on February 27 he and the rest of the Conservative caucus voted yea on an amendment to the second-reading motion, which was defeated 41–48 by the government and Green members, and on March 13 he voted yea on two committee amendments moved by Conservative MLA Steve Kooner (to clauses 5 and 39), both defeated by the government majority (38–47 and 38–48). The bill became law with Royal Assent on March 31, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M202.purpose: A private member's bill from NDP MLA Darlene Rotchford that disqualifies a sitting MLA from also holding a local elected office. Her stated aim was that people can be confident their representatives are not collecting two paycheques or in a conflict of interest, bringing BC in line with Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba and Ontario.
43rd1st:Bill M202.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (48–42), at report stage twice (46–42 and 48–41) and on the government's motion to recommit the bill to the Select Standing Committee on Private Bills (48–42), each time with the whole voting Conservative caucus, while the NDP and the two Green members voted yea. He did not speak on the bill, and no statement of his reasons is on the record. It passed because the NDP and Green members together outnumbered the Conservatives, and it received Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M204.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Jody Toor that requires the minister to develop a strategy to support perinatal and postnatal mental health in BC. She argued that about one in five women in BC experience perinatal or postnatal mental health struggles, and that too many suffer in silence without support.
43rd1st:Bill M204.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading on March 10, 2025. The vote was unanimous, 91–0, with the full Conservative caucus and every other voting member in favour, so no one opposed it. It was his own caucus colleague's bill, and he did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote itself. The bill went on to pass third reading in May and received Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 8.purpose: Ends the consumer carbon tax in BC. It cancels all scheduled rate increases and sets the carbon tax rate to zero dollars per tonne as of April 1, 2025, and ends the climate action tax credit after the final payments in April, with other amendments, including a refund and crediting mechanism for natural gas retail dealers. Introduced by Finance Minister Brenda Bailey (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 8.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading (89–1) and at second reading (88–2), and nay on an amendment to the second-reading motion that only the two Green members supported (defeated 2–89). In his speech he said the Conservatives supported eliminating the carbon tax, but credited Conservative pressure across the country for forcing the government's reversal, quoted the Premier's earlier statements that the tax was essential, and called it an NDP policy abandoned only under pressure. He asked where the lost revenue would be made up given the deficit, and said same-day Royal Assent showed that Part 4 of Bill 7 was an overreach. It passed because the NDP and Conservatives both backed ending the tax (only the two Green members voted against at second reading), and it received Royal Assent the same day, March 31, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 7.purpose: Gives the government new powers to respond to the threat of US tariffs. It lets government reduce interprovincial trade barriers, issue procurement directives to public-sector bodies, and impose tolls, fees or charges on certain vehicles, and it lets cabinet modify laws and authorizations by regulation to respond to the tariffs (Part 4). Sponsored by Attorney General Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 7.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (48–43), on three committee clauses and at third reading (48–44), with the whole voting Conservative caucus; and yea on Conservative amendments to clauses 3 and 6, both defeated 5–7. He did not speak on Bill 7 itself, but in later debate he called Part 4 sweeping, non-democratic legislation and an overreach of power, and described Bill 14 as 'Bill 7 in disguise' and a power grab, which points to his objection being the breadth of cabinet's power to change laws by regulation rather than the tariff response itself. It passed because the NDP members, with the Greens, outvoted the Conservatives, and became law with Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M208.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Macklin McCall that would require the minister of emergency management to set up a committee to develop a provincial volunteer organization, the BC Volunteer Corps, to encourage volunteering and create a central platform where people can find volunteer opportunities for emergencies.
43rd1st:Bill M208.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading, and he spoke in support on April 7, 2025. He said the bill was simple but powerful, drew on the 2023 wildfire season in the north Shuswap, where local volunteers did boat rescues and delivered supplies without structure, training or recognition, and said rural and remote regions like his know what works on the ground and should be part of designing the corps. The bill was defeated 45–46 on April 14: the Conservatives and the two Greens voted for it and all 46 NDP members voted against, so the government's votes decided it by one.

43rd1st:Bill M212.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative leader John Rustad, titled the Grocery Rebate Guarantee, that raises the basic personal amount in BC's Income Tax Act from $9,713 to $22,462, which would raise the amount of income people can earn before paying provincial income tax.
43rd1st:Bill M212.vote_analysis: The only recorded vote is first reading, the formal introduction, which he supported (yea, 90–1, with almost every member in favour, since first reading is normally allowed without debate). Because it never reached second reading, there is no debate or later vote, and he did not speak to it, so his own reasons are not on the record. It was his party leader's bill and the Conservative caucus supported it. It was not brought forward for further stages.

43rd1st:Bill M211.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Hon Chan that repeals BC's Zero-Emission Vehicles Act, which sets a 2035 ban on sales of new gas-powered vehicles, along with its fines and potential jail time. He called it the consumer choice amendment act and argued that it does not ban electric vehicles, only the mandate.
43rd1st:Bill M211.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading and spoke strongly in support on May 5, 2025. He argued from his rural riding: an electric truck at about $85,000 before taxes for an Enderby contractor, winter range cut in half, no charging near forestry roads, and limited transit in places like Blind Bay and Seymour Arm, where a 90-minute drive to the hospital means a personal vehicle is a lifeline and a safety issue. He said the bill protects consumer choice and trusts British Columbians rather than parenting them. It was defeated 44–47, with the Conservatives for it and the NDP and Greens against.

43rd1st:Bill M213.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Steve Kooner that provides for drug use prevention education in BC schools, including mandatory anti-drug messaging.
43rd1st:Bill M213.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading (92–0, unanimous, May 6, 2025) and at second reading (October 27, 2025), which was defeated 43–48. All 43 voting Conservatives were for it, and the NDP and Green members voted against, so the government side defeated it. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record beyond supporting a bill from his own caucus.

43rd1st:Bill 5.purpose: Implements the 2025 provincial budget's measures. Part 1 allows the government to forecast budget deficits through the 2027–28 fiscal year, and Part 2 amends a dozen or more statutes (including the Income Tax Act, School Act, Taxation (Rural Area) Act and Speculation and Vacancy Tax Act), with tax credits for film and animation production, apprenticeship credits, a higher small-business venture capital credit cap and changes to who oversees BC Assessment's bylaws. Introduced by Finance Minister Brenda Bailey (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 5.vote_analysis: He voted yea on an amendment to the second-reading motion (defeated 41–48, with the Conservatives for and the NDP and Greens against) and yea on second reading itself, which passed unanimously, 89–0, on May 6, 2025. In his April 16 speech he described 'cautious support with rural reservations': he welcomed the apprenticeship credits and keeping the BC family benefit for six months after a child's death, but questioned moving BC Assessment bylaw oversight to Treasury Board, said venture-capital credits mostly help urban investors, said the speculation tax does not fit rural vacancy, and said the deficit-forecast extension showed a government 'moving the goalposts'. On April 17 he urged members to pass an amendment, arguing from the cost of groceries. The bill received Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M214.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Misty Van Popta, the Firefighters' Health Act. It requires a plan for comprehensive health screening of firefighters, to be tabled in the Legislature and reviewed every five years. Its sponsor noted that both the government and opposition committed to supporting firefighters in the fall 2024 campaign.
43rd1st:Bill M214.vote_analysis: His only recorded vote is yea on May 12, 2025 on the motion to place the bill on the Orders of the Day for second reading at the next sitting, which carried unanimously, 91–0, so no one opposed taking it up. He did not speak on the bill, and no statement of his reasons is on the record. According to the Legislature's progress of bills it was read a second time but did not receive a third reading in that session.

43rd1st:Bill 11.purpose: Changes the Employment Standards Act so that employers may not require sick notes for short health-related leaves. The goal was twofold: ease the administrative burden on doctors and other health care providers so they can spend their time on patients, and remove the burden on workers of having to provide a note for a short absence. Introduced by Labour Minister Jennifer Whiteside (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 11.vote_analysis: He voted yea at third reading on May 12, 2025, and the vote was unanimous, 91–0. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; a unanimous vote shows it had support across the House. It received Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 15.purpose: Creates the Infrastructure Projects Act, giving the new Ministry of Infrastructure powers for policy, planning, procurement, delivery and oversight of major public-sector infrastructure. It lets cabinet designate types of projects and apply streamlining options to designated projects. Introduced by Infrastructure Minister Bowinn Ma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 15.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (46–44) and third reading (46–46), and yea on Conservative committee amendments by Trevor Halford, Kiel Giddens and Misty Van Popta, all defeated 5–7 or 6–6. He did not speak on Bill 15 and his reasons are not on the record. The nearest evidence is his Bill 14 speech the same month, which called that streamlining bill a power grab; both bills were put through a single time-allocation motion that he also voted against. It passed because all 46 NDP members voted yes at second reading, outnumbering the Conservatives and the two Greens, and at third reading the vote was tied 46–46 and carried; the Speaker votes only to break a tie. Several committee votes were tied 6–6 and decided by the chair. It received Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 14.purpose: Makes the BC Energy Regulator the main permitting body for renewable energy projects and major transmission lines, lets it set a new regulatory framework for renewable projects at one of three levels of intensity, and exempts some projects, such as wind power projects, from the Environmental Assessment Act. Introduced by Energy and Climate Solutions Minister Adrian Dix (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 14.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (46–43) and third reading (46–46). In his May 8, 2025 speech he said he supports renewable energy but not 'a blank cheque' for unaccountable regulators to rewrite rules, suspend safety standards and override property rights. He objected that cabinet could prescribe other energy sources as renewable, said the bill centralizes authority and carries consequences for workers, landowners and communities, wanted more consultation, and said it should not pick winners and losers. He called it 'Bill 7 in disguise' and a power grab, and said he could not support it in its current form. It passed second reading because all 46 NDP members voted yea against the Conservatives and the two Greens, and passed third reading on a tied 46–46 vote; the Speaker votes only to break a tie. It received Royal Assent on May 29, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 16.purpose: The 2025 Supply Act. It authorizes the government to spend the funds needed to operate government programs in the 2025–26 fiscal year, following the House's approval of the main estimates. Introduced by Finance Minister Brenda Bailey (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 16.vote_analysis: He voted nay at third reading on May 29, 2025, with all 44 voting Conservatives, while the NDP and the two Green members voted yea. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; opposition parties conventionally vote against a supply bill to register opposition to the government's spending plan. It passed 48–44 because the NDP and Green members outnumbered the Conservatives, and it received Royal Assent the same day.

43rd1st:Protecting Minors from Gender Tr.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong, who left the Conservative caucus in 2025. Its title and her introduction describe a bill to stop doctors providing puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and surgeries to children, and schools socially transitioning children with new names and pronouns, which she argued cause irreversible harm.
43rd1st:Protecting Minors from Gender Tr.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on October 8, 2025, which was defeated 40–48: 40 Conservatives voted for it and the NDP and Green members, with one Conservative, voted against. A bill is rarely defeated at first reading, when members are normally allowing it to be introduced. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill 17.purpose: Keeps the intimate images protection service running. It continues the authority of the service, which gives people a fast and accessible way to stop the non-consensual sharing of intimate images, and the indirect collection of personal information needed to support its clients, and lets cabinet set a monetary limit for certain Civil Resolution Tribunal claims. Introduced by Attorney General Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 17.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading on October 9, 2025, which passed unanimously, 87–0. He did not speak on the bill, and no reasons are on the record; a unanimous vote shows support from every party in the House. It received Royal Assent on October 30, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 12.purpose: Amends the Motor Vehicle Act to make driver licensing more accessible and safe. It creates new authorities to update the restrictions, qualifications and timelines under the graduated licensing program and the new motorcyclist licensing program, including ICBC's role in testing and wait times and a ban on electronic device use for learner motorcyclists. Introduced by Garry Begg (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 12.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading on October 9, 2025, which passed unanimously, 85–0, while speaking critically. He said the essence of the bill is good but it is 'not without its flaws' and 'inequities'. He objected that it gives ICBC and cabinet sweeping power to change licensing requirements by regulation, which should be debated in the House with public consultation, and that it treats rural and urban drivers unfairly: a young person from Grindrod needing to drive to work should not be penalized by distance from an ICBC training centre. He proposed legislated public consultation before new licensing rules take effect. The bill passed unanimously and received Royal Assent on October 30, 2025.

43rd1st:Land Acknowledgement Prohibition.purpose: A private member's bill from Dallas Brodie (OneBC, elected as a Conservative). Per her introduction, it would make it unlawful for publicly funded institutions and their employees, such as teachers, to make or require land acknowledgements that deny the Crown's sovereignty over the lands of British Columbia or attribute collective guilt based on race, ancestry or historical actions. She said it protects historically accurate statements and academic freedom.
43rd1st:Land Acknowledgement Prohibition.vote_analysis: He voted nay at first reading on October 23, 2025, and it was defeated 5–85: only five Conservatives voted for it, and he was among the 37 Conservatives who voted with the NDP and Greens to reject it. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill 18.purpose: Replaces the Sexual Violence and Misconduct Policy Act with a new Sexual Violence Policy Act for public post-secondary institutions, replacing the term 'sexual misconduct' with 'sexual violence' and modernizing requirements so institutions' policies and procedures meet best practices for prevention and trauma-informed response. Introduced by Jessie Sunner (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 18.vote_analysis: He voted yea at third reading on October 23, 2025, and it passed unanimously, 87–0. He did not speak on the bill, and no reasons are on the record; a unanimous vote shows support from all parties. It received Royal Assent on October 30, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 19.purpose: Expands the child care that school boards may provide on school property, beyond the current limit of before- and after-school care for enrolled students on school days, and lets boards recoup reasonable fees for it. Introduced by Education and Child Care Minister Lisa Beare (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 19.vote_analysis: He voted yea at third reading on October 27, 2025, which passed unanimously, 90–0, and yea on a committee amendment to clause 2.1 moved by Conservative MLA Scott McInnis, which was defeated 3–6. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; the pattern is support for the bill, with a Conservative amendment the government members did not accept. It received Royal Assent on October 30, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 31.purpose: Amends the Hydro and Power Authority Act and the Utilities Commission Act. It lets BC Hydro enter co-ownership arrangements with First Nations for parts of the North Coast transmission line, lets BC Hydro keep its rights while acting for a limited partnership, and changes the Utilities Commission Act so government can decide which large new industrial users get access to electricity. Introduced by Energy Minister Adrian Dix (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 31.vote_analysis: He voted yea on the six-month hoist amendment (defeated 40–48), nay at second reading (48–42) and third reading (46–46), nay on clauses 1 and 2, and yea on most of the committee amendments to clauses 1 and 2 moved by Larry Neufeld and Jeremy Valeriote, all of which were defeated. He spoke at length. He said it was 'short on paper but long on consequences': it gave more control but no capacity guarantee, replaced consultation with cabinet discretion, weakened BC Utilities Commission oversight of public assets, and was 'not a good bill' as written, and he wanted it brought back with guardrails. He said BC Hydro already had the authority to build the line, and supported Indigenous partnership in principle. In committee he asked about valuation if a stake were sold, whether a private equity group could buy in, cybersecurity, and whether cabinet designations override the Utilities Commission Act. It passed second reading because the NDP and the two Greens outvoted the Conservatives, and passed third reading on a tied 46–46 vote, which the Speaker breaks by voting; the Greens voted against it there. It received Royal Assent on November 27, 2025.

43rd1st:Property Rights Protection Act.purpose: A private member's bill introduced by Dallas Brodie (OneBC, elected as a Conservative). No bill text or introduction statement was found in the legislative records reviewed, so its content cannot be described beyond its title, which concerns the protection of property rights.
43rd1st:Property Rights Protection Act.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on October 29, 2025, which was defeated 40–48: 40 Conservatives voted for it and the NDP and Green members voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:New Resident Health Cost Recover.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent). It would require new residents who are not yet Canadian citizens or permanent residents to pay an annual health registration fee of $7,500 per person as a condition of coverage under the Medicare Protection Act, adjusted for inflation and ending when they become permanent residents or citizens, with revenue held in a dedicated account. She argued that the fee reflects the average annual cost of publicly funded care in BC.
43rd1st:New Resident Health Cost Recover.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on October 30, 2025, which was defeated 37–48: 37 Conservatives voted for it and the NDP and Green members voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill 30.purpose: Adds a new unpaid, job-protected leave to the Employment Standards Act for employees dealing with a serious personal illness or injury: up to 27 weeks within any 52-week period. Introduced by Labour Minister Jennifer Whiteside (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 30.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading on October 30, 2025, which passed 81–2; the two nay votes were Conservatives, so he sided with the large majority of his caucus (33 voting Conservatives) and the NDP and Greens. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. It received Royal Assent on November 27, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M216.purpose: A private member's bill from NDP MLA George Anderson, the Professional Reliance Act. It aims to streamline development projects and reduce administrative costs in local government approvals, so that qualified, provincially regulated professionals do not have their work reviewed multiple times.
43rd1st:Bill M216.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading on November 17, 2025, along with 42 other Conservatives and the two Greens; it passed 47–44 because all 46 NDP members and one Conservative voted yea. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. According to the Legislature's progress of bills it did not go on to third reading.

43rd1st:Bill 25.purpose: Amends the Local Government Act, the Vancouver Charter and the Short-Term Rental Accommodations Act to remove barriers to small-scale, multi-unit housing by clarifying and expanding where that type of housing must be allowed. It also adds regulation-making and exemption powers for cabinet. Introduced by Housing Minister Christine Boyle (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 25.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (48–44) with all 44 voting Conservatives, nay on committee amendments to clauses 4 and 9, and nay on clauses 10, 22, 25 and 33. His only recorded remark was a question in committee on November 20, 2025, asking the minister what the purpose of one change was. Beyond that his reasons are not on the record. It passed because the NDP and the two Greens outnumbered the Conservatives, and received Royal Assent on November 27, 2025.

43rd1st:Declaration on the Rights of Ind.purpose: A private member's bill from Jordan Kealy (elected as a Conservative, then an Independent) that would repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA). In his introduction he said that reconciliation matters but that DRIPA as implemented is dividing people, creating uncertainty about land decisions and unequal treatment of children in the same family, and eroding trust.
43rd1st:Declaration on the Rights of Ind.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on November 19, 2025, which was defeated 43–48: all 43 voting Conservatives were for it and the NDP and Green members voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Post-Secondary Institutions Dive.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent). By her introduction it bans race-based hiring, identity quotas and ideological litmus tests at publicly funded universities, with institutions that refuse to comply losing their funding. She argued that diversity, equity and inclusion programs award jobs on race or sex instead of merit.
43rd1st:Post-Secondary Institutions Dive.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on November 19, 2025, which was defeated 41–50: 41 Conservatives voted for it, and the NDP, the Greens and two Conservatives voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill 20.purpose: The Construction Prompt Payment Act sets up a scheme for prompt payment and timely, accessible adjudication of disputes in the construction industry, so workers and subcontractors who supply services or materials on construction projects are paid on time. Introduced by Attorney General Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 20.vote_analysis: His only recorded division is a committee vote on clause 42 on November 19, 2025, where he voted yea and the vote was unanimous, 87–0. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. It received Royal Assent on November 27, 2025.

43rd1st:National Day for Truth and Recon.purpose: A private member's bill from Dallas Brodie (OneBC, elected as a Conservative) that would repeal the statute establishing the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation as a holiday in BC. In her introduction she said the day does not deserve to be a holiday, disputed the findings of the Kamloops Indian Residential School site, and said Canadians have no wrongdoing to reconcile.
43rd1st:National Day for Truth and Recon.vote_analysis: He voted nay at first reading on November 20, 2025, which was defeated 3–86: only three Conservatives voted for it, and he was among the 38 who voted with the NDP and Greens against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill M217.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Ward Stamer, the Dashboard Cameras in Commercial Vehicles Act. It requires mandatory installation and operation of dashboard cameras in commercial vehicles, which he said is a step toward safety and accountability on roads.
43rd1st:Bill M217.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading on November 24, 2025, which passed unanimously, 91–0, so it had the support of every party. It was a Conservative colleague's bill, and he did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It was reinstated in the next session and became law (see its entry in 2026).

43rd1st:Public Flags Display Act.purpose: A private member's bill from Dallas Brodie (OneBC, elected as a Conservative). By her introduction it would prohibit flying any flags on provincial property other than the Canadian flag, the BC flag and municipal flags, which she said would stop other flags replacing them on public buildings, giving as examples the Palestinian flag and a transgender flag at the Legislature.
43rd1st:Public Flags Display Act.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on November 25, 2025, which was defeated 15–73. The Conservative caucus split: 15 voted for it and 25 against, so he was in the minority of his own caucus, and the NDP and Greens voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill 32.purpose: Amends the Mental Health Act to replace the 'deemed consent' provision in section 31(1) with a more explicit and robust liability shield for providers of authorized professional services, care and treatment. Introduced by Health Minister Josie Osborne (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 32.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (46–46) and third reading (45–41), and yea on committee amendments moved by Conservative Claire Rattée and Green leader Jeremy Valeriote, all defeated. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; his votes show a pattern of trying to amend rather than support it. At second reading the NDP's 46 votes tied the Conservatives' 44 plus the Greens' 2 and the motion carried, the Speaker breaking ties. At third reading 45 NDP members outvoted 40 Conservatives and one Green. It received Royal Assent on December 3, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill 24.purpose: Lets the government recover health care costs caused by vaping products, giving the province the opportunity to recoup some of the health care expenses it must incur because of the harms vaping products cause, through legal action against the companies involved. Introduced by Attorney General Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 24.vote_analysis: He voted yea on three committee amendments to clause 1 (defeated 3–5) and nay at third reading (49–42), with the whole voting Conservative caucus except one. In his October 22, 2025 speech he opened with his own experience: a smoker for most of his adult life who lost his wife of 38 years to lung cancer and later vaped, believing it safer. He said the bill was 'far from perfect' but 'necessary, proactive and pragmatic' and that 'we are prepared to support' it, while urging the government not to turn it into a political cash grab or use it to fill budget gaps. The record does not say why he then voted nay at third reading; the amendments he supported in committee had been defeated in between. It passed 49–42 with the NDP and Greens, and received Royal Assent on December 3, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M225.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent), the Secure Procurement in Respect of China Act. It prohibits public bodies from contracting for goods or services from suppliers meeting certain criteria with respect to the People's Republic of China, if comparable goods or services are available elsewhere.
43rd1st:Bill M225.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on November 26, 2025, which passed 84–4: the NDP, the Greens and 36 Conservatives voted for it and four Conservatives voted against. First reading is normally the formal introduction of a bill. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not advance beyond first reading.

43rd1st:Bill 29.purpose: Amends the Child, Family and Community Service Act, the framework for BC's child-protection system, with changes about safety plans: voluntary, short-term, collaborative plans between a child's parents and ministry staff, used in the early stages of a child-protection response while an assessment or investigation is underway. Introduced by Children and Family Development Minister Jodie Wickens (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 29.vote_analysis: He voted yea on five amendments to clauses 3 and 6 moved by Conservative MLA Rosalyn Bird (all defeated, most by about 40–48 or 42–48, with the NDP and Greens against). He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; the pattern is a caucus effort to change the bill's safety-plan provisions through amendment, none of which the government accepted. The bill received Royal Assent on December 3, 2025.

43rd1st:Bill M219.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Anna Kindy, the Health Authorities Amendment Act. It requires health authorities to determine the medically recommended time period for health services, to notify a patient when they will not receive services for a serious medical condition within that period, and to report on it, aiming at transparency about wait times.
43rd1st:Bill M219.vote_analysis: He voted yea on second reading on December 2, 2025, which was defeated 43–48 with the Conservatives for and the NDP and Greens against, after he voted nay on December 1 on a government motion to further defer the division (it passed 48–40). He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond supporting a bill from his own caucus. It did not proceed.

43rd1st:Bill M228.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent) that designates March 11 as Freedom Convoy Recognition Day and makes it a public holiday and a statutory holiday under the Employment Standards Act. She said it recognizes the achievements of what she called one of the largest peaceful demonstrations in Canadian history.
43rd1st:Bill M228.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on December 2, 2025, which passed 87–2: the NDP and 41 Conservatives were for it and only the two Green members voted against. First reading is normally the formal introduction of a bill. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not advance beyond first reading.

43rd1st:Bill 28.purpose: Gives people in BC tools to protect themselves against credit fraud, specifically security alerts and credit freezes, and improves their access to the personal information held about them by credit reporting agencies. Introduced by Attorney General Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd1st:Bill 28.vote_analysis: He voted yea on a committee amendment to clause 6 moved by Conservative MLA Steve Kooner on December 3, 2025, which was defeated 38–46 with the NDP voting against. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; his only recorded vote was to change the bill rather than oppose it. It received Royal Assent the same day, December 3, 2025.

43rd2nd:Gender Ideology and Child Protec.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent). In her introduction she said it would classify the promotion of gender ideology as a form of emotional harm under the Family Law Act and the Child, Family and Community Service Act, ban social transition in schools, require schools to inform parents of identity changes, restrict access to opposite-sex bathrooms, and remove related materials from libraries and classrooms.
43rd2nd:Gender Ideology and Child Protec.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on February 19, 2026, which was defeated 38–49: 38 Conservatives voted for it and the NDP, the Greens and one Conservative voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd2nd:Bill M226.purpose: A private member's bill from NDP MLA Dana Lajeunesse, the Motor Vehicle Amendment Act (No. 2), 2025. It adds a definition and prohibition for reckless driving, requires peace officers to report reckless driving to the superintendent of motor vehicles, lets the superintendent act on it and creates an offence for driving while prohibited for reckless driving.
43rd2nd:Bill M226.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading on February 23, 2026, and it passed 78–7: the NDP, the Greens and 30 Conservatives voted yea and only seven Conservatives, including him, voted nay, so he was in a small minority of his own caucus. He did not speak. In the same debate, Conservative MLA Korky Neufeld said he had problems with vague wording such as 'driving as close as possible to another vehicle' and with unintended consequences, which is the stated concern from within his caucus. It did not go on to third reading according to the Legislature's progress of bills.

43rd2nd:Human Rights Code Repeal Act.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent) that would repeal the BC Human Rights Code. In her introduction she said its purpose is to end what she called the assault on freedom of speech by the Human Rights Tribunal, citing a recent large fine against a person for expressing personal opinions.
43rd2nd:Human Rights Code Repeal Act.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on February 26, 2026, which was defeated 37–50: 37 Conservatives voted for it, and the NDP, the Greens and two Conservatives voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd2nd:Bill 3.purpose: Implements further measures from the 2026 budget. It establishes a new British Columbia Strategic Investments special account to advance economic opportunities with partners such as the federal government. Introduced by Finance Minister Brenda Bailey (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 3.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (48–43) and third reading (46–42), each time with the Conservative caucus, with the NDP voting yea at both stages and the Greens supporting second reading and opposing third. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. It passed because the NDP, with the Greens at second reading, outvoted the Conservatives, and it received Royal Assent on March 12, 2026.

43rd2nd:Bill M235.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent), the Drug Recovery and Community Safety Act. It requires cancellation of authorization and provincial funding for facilities that permit the use of controlled substances and requires a plan to redirect that money to recovery, which she introduced as 'if we want to fight drugs, we shouldn't pay people to use them.'
43rd2nd:Bill M235.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on March 5, 2026, which passed 84–2: the NDP and 39 Conservatives were for it and only the two Greens voted against. First reading is normally the formal introduction of a bill. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not advance beyond first reading.

43rd2nd:Bill 5.purpose: The Trade Recognition Act replaces Part 1 of the Economic Stabilization (Tariff Response) Act. It reduces internal trade barriers by recognizing other provinces' regulations: a good that may be sold or used in another province may be sold or used in BC, and likewise a service, unless an exception applies, while preserving BC's ability to apply rules on health, safety, consumer and environmental protection. Introduced by Ravi Kahlon (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 5.vote_analysis: His only recorded division is a committee vote on March 5, 2026, where he voted yea on an amendment to clause 7 moved by Green leader Jeremy Valeriote; it was tied 5–5 and defeated, with the NDP members voting against and the chair deciding the tie. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. The bill received Royal Assent on March 12, 2026.

43rd2nd:Bill 2.purpose: Implements the 2026 budget's measures. Part 1 amends eight statutes, including the Balanced Budget and Ministerial Accountability Act, Financial Administration Act and FOIPPA, and Part 2 amends the homeowner grant, Income Tax, Provincial Sales Tax, Property Transfer Tax, School and Speculation and Vacancy Tax statutes to implement the tax measures announced in Budget 2026, with technical tax changes. Introduced by Finance Minister Brenda Bailey (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 2.vote_analysis: He voted nay at second reading (46–45) and third reading (46–46), with the Conservative caucus and the two Greens opposed at both. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. Both votes were close: the 46 NDP members carried second reading by one vote, and third reading was tied 46–46 and carried, the Speaker breaking ties. It received Royal Assent on April 16, 2026.

43rd2nd:Defunding Aboriginal Title Claim.purpose: A private member's bill from Tara Armstrong (elected as a Conservative, since an Independent). By her introduction it would suspend non-essential provincial funding to any Indigenous group that has begun an Aboriginal title claim affecting private property in BC, and prohibit provincial funding being used to support such claims. She named the Cowichan Tribes and the Tk'emlúps te Secwépemc as groups it would affect.
43rd2nd:Defunding Aboriginal Title Claim.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on March 12, 2026, which was defeated 38–49: 38 Conservatives voted for it and the NDP, the Greens and one Conservative voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd2nd:Bill 6.purpose: Supports the first phase of modernizing driver licensing, a ten-year program to protect online licensing services, modernize ICBC's processes and technology and connect with government services. It allows online applications for simple licence renewals and for replacing lost, destroyed or damaged licences, and clarifies authority to exempt fees. Introduced by Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 6.vote_analysis: He voted yea at third reading on April 1, 2026, which passed unanimously, 92–0. He did not speak on the bill, and no reasons are on the record; a unanimous vote shows it had support in every party. It received Royal Assent on April 16, 2026.

43rd2nd:Bill 12.purpose: Extends the Safe Access to Schools Act, which lets cabinet establish access zones around K–12 schools in which certain disruptive or harmful behaviours are prohibited, from its repeal date of July 1, 2026 to July 1, 2028. The government's stated purpose is to protect students and staff from the effects of protests at schools. Introduced by Niki Sharma (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 12.vote_analysis: He voted yea at third reading on April 1, 2026, which passed 86–4: the NDP, the Greens and 38 Conservatives voted for it, and four Conservatives voted against. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. It received Royal Assent on April 16, 2026.

43rd2nd:Bill M241.purpose: A private member's bill from Elenore Sturko (then Conservative, now CentreBC leader) that repeals section 8.1 of the Interpretation Act, added in 2021, which requires every act and regulation to be interpreted consistently with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. She noted that the section was relied on in the Cowichan Tribes v. Canada decision on Aboriginal title.
43rd2nd:Bill M241.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on April 13, 2026, which passed unanimously, 92–0; first reading is normally the formal introduction of a bill. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not advance beyond first reading.

43rd2nd:Bill M233.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Kiel Giddens, the Public Sector Construction Projects Procurement Act. It prohibits issuing solicitations for public sector construction projects that require, or have the effect of requiring, successful vendors to employ unionized or non-unionized employees. A supporting speaker argued it responds to higher costs and delays under community benefits agreements.
43rd2nd:Bill M233.vote_analysis: He voted yea at second reading on April 20, 2026, which was defeated 42–48: the Conservatives voted for it and the NDP and the Greens voted against. He did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond supporting a bill from his own caucus. It did not proceed.

43rd2nd:Bill 14.purpose: Amends the Forest Act and the Forest and Range Practices Act. The Forest Act changes concern the BC Timber Sales account, which governs how BC Timber Sales may use its funds, with the stated aim of transforming BC Timber Sales into a modern, adaptable partner of choice amid wildfire threats, US duties and tariffs, low lumber prices and the end of the pine beetle harvest. Introduced by Forests Minister Ravi Parmar (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 14.vote_analysis: He voted yea at third reading on April 21, 2026, which passed unanimously, 89–0. He did not speak on the bill, and no reasons are on the record; a unanimous vote shows support in every party. It received Royal Assent on May 21, 2026.

43rd2nd:Declaration on the Rights of Ind.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Trevor Halford that would repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA). In his introduction he said that when it passed in 2019 British Columbians were promised it would not cast doubt on private property, create a veto over development or be used to strike down laws, and that it has done all three, citing the Premier's own description of the legal risk.
43rd2nd:Declaration on the Rights of Ind.vote_analysis: He voted yea at first reading on April 22, 2026, which was defeated 44–47: all 44 voting Conservatives were for it and the NDP and Greens voted against. It was a bill introduced by his own caucus, and he did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It did not proceed.

43rd2nd:Bill M237.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Sheldon Clare, the Insurance (Vehicle) Amendment Act, 2026. It extends the time within which a person can make a claim for benefits for a catastrophic injury under the Insurance (Vehicle) Act. In introducing it he gave the example of a motorcyclist who lost a leg in a crash on Highway 97.
43rd2nd:Bill M237.vote_analysis: His only recorded vote is nay on April 22, 2026 on the government's motion that, if the bill passes second reading, it be committed to the Special Committee to Review Provisions of the Insurance (Vehicle) Act. It passed 49–42 with the NDP, the Greens and two Conservatives voting yea and 42 Conservatives voting nay. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; the vote was against sending his own caucus's bill to a special committee, not on the bill itself.

43rd2nd:Bill M217.purpose: A private member's bill from Conservative MLA Ward Stamer, the Dashboard Cameras in Commercial Vehicles Act, which requires mandatory installation and operation of dashboard cameras in commercial vehicles. Reinstated from the previous session, where it had passed second reading unanimously.
43rd2nd:Bill M217.vote_analysis: He voted yea on May 4, 2026 on the report stage motion, which passed unanimously, 90–0. The bill's sponsor said the committee had improved it and that its main purpose was road safety. He did not speak on it himself, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote. It passed third reading on May 25 and received Royal Assent on May 28, 2026, which makes it a rare private member's bill that became law.

43rd2nd:Bill 9.purpose: Amends the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FOIPPA), BC's access-to-information and privacy law, to keep it working in a modern digital environment. The government says it supports more connected, people-centred services while protecting privacy, adds efficiencies in how FOI requests are processed, and responds to recommendations of the Information and Privacy Commissioner and past special committees. Specific changes include letting a public body extend the response time with the applicant's consent and letting it refuse to disclose communications by a judicial officer about policy. Introduced by Citizens' Services Minister Diana Gibson (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 9.vote_analysis: He voted nay on second reading (48–42) and third reading (46–46) and yea on a six-month hoist amendment (defeated 42–48), and nay on the government's motion to limit debate and its procedural motions. He spoke against it on March 4 and 10 and again in support of the hoist on May 6, 2026. He said the bill is 'nothing like the title indicates': it shifts power from citizens to government discretion, normalizes delay and refusal, weakens the Information and Privacy Commissioner's oversight, sets vague thresholds, and creates fees that would 'paywall' transparency and penalize low-income applicants, harming journalists, researchers and watchdogs, and he said 'access delayed is often access denied'. He cited criticism from the Freedom of Information and Privacy Association and the Canadian Association of Journalists. It passed because the NDP's 46 votes carried second reading 48–42, and third reading was tied 46–46 and carried, the Speaker breaking ties. It received Royal Assent on May 28, 2026.

43rd2nd:Bill 20.purpose: Enacts the K'ómoks Treaty Act and related amendments, satisfying the province's obligation under the K'ómoks Treaty to pass legislation giving effect to and ratifying the treaty. Introduced by Spencer Chandra Herbert (NDP), with the K'ómoks First Nations delegation present.
43rd2nd:Bill 20.vote_analysis: He voted yea on a six-month hoist amendment to the second-reading motion (defeated 44–48), nay at second reading (48–42) and nay at third reading, which passed 53–39. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record. It passed because the NDP carried it with the Greens at second reading and, at third reading, five Conservatives joined the NDP and Greens, leaving 39 Conservatives, including him, opposed. It received Royal Assent on May 28, 2026.

43rd2nd:Bill 22.purpose: The 2026 Supply Act. It authorizes the government to spend the funds needed to operate government programs in the 2026–27 fiscal year, following the House's approval of the main estimates. Introduced by Finance Minister Brenda Bailey (NDP).
43rd2nd:Bill 22.vote_analysis: He voted nay at third reading on May 28, 2026, with 43 other Conservatives and the two Greens, while the 46 NDP members voted yea. He did not speak on the bill, so his reasons are not on the record; opposition parties conventionally vote against a supply bill to register opposition to the government's spending plan. It passed by one vote, 46–45, and received Royal Assent the same day.

43rd1st:Motion 7.purpose: A motion from NDP MLA Jennifer Blatherwick. It condemns President Trump's proposed tariffs as wrong and unjustified measures threatening Canadian sovereignty, and endorses the nationally coordinated 'Team Canada' plan to respond with proportionate retaliatory action if necessary, including targeting industries and regions such as products from Republican states.
43rd1st:Motion 7.vote_analysis: He voted yea on February 24, 2025, and it passed 86–5: the NDP, the two Greens and 38 Conservatives voted for it and five Conservatives voted against, so he was with most of his caucus. He did not speak on the motion, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote.

43rd1st:Motion 18.purpose: A government motion moved by Hon. Tamara Davidson (NDP). The House acknowledges the findings of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls that cultural genocide occurred in Canada, recognizes residential schools as a key pillar of that strategy, recognizes decades of legal precedent affirming Indigenous rights and title, and accepts that survivors' voices must be at the centre of discussion.
43rd1st:Motion 18.vote_analysis: He voted yea on April 14, 2025, and it was agreed unanimously, 92–0, with every member who voted in favour. He did not speak on the motion, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote.

43rd2nd:Motion 13.purpose: A government motion moved by Hon. Mike Farnworth (NDP) that the House affirms its unequivocal support for the BC Human Rights Code and the Tribunal's powers to enforce it, protecting people from hate speech and discrimination on listed grounds such as Indigenous identity, race, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression and age. Conservative MLA Á’a:líya Warbus moved an amendment replacing everything after 'Human Rights Code' with 'and protecting all people from hate and discrimination'.
43rd2nd:Motion 13.vote_analysis: He voted yea on the amendment, which was defeated 36–50 (the NDP, the Greens and two Conservatives voted against), then yea on the main motion, which passed 83–3 on March 12, 2026, with all but three voting Conservatives joining the NDP and Greens. He did not speak on the motion, so his reasons are not on the record; the pattern is to try to change the wording and then support the motion.

43rd2nd:Motion M 203.purpose: A private member's motion from Conservative MLA Tony Luck that the House affirms that the application of the merit principle within the BC Public Service be overseen by an independent officer of the Legislature.
43rd2nd:Motion M 203.vote_analysis: He voted yea on March 31, 2026, and it was defeated 45–46: the Conservatives and the two Greens voted for it and all 46 NDP members voted against, so the government side defeated it by one vote. It was a Conservative colleague's motion, and he did not speak on it, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the vote.

43rd2nd:Motion M 205.purpose: A private member's motion from Conservative MLA Gavin Dew asking the Legislative Assembly Management Committee to institute a mandatory course in economics, public finance and numeracy for all newly elected MLAs as part of orientation, so representatives are accountable and supported to understand the policy decisions on taxes, spending, debt and regulation. NDP MLA Jennifer Blatherwick amended it to add 'public policy implications, including evidence-based science, truth and reconciliation, and human rights', and Conservative Kiel Giddens moved a subamendment to delete that added text.
43rd2nd:Motion M 205.vote_analysis: He voted yea on the subamendment (April 27, 2026), which was tied 45–45 and defeated when the Speaker, by established practice, voted against it, and nay on the amendment (May 4), which passed 46–45 with the NDP for it and the Conservatives and Greens against. So he voted to strip the added text from his colleague's motion, and lost narrowly twice. The motion as amended was agreed 48–40 on May 25, 2026, a division in which he is not listed. He did not speak on the motion, so his reasons are not on the record beyond the votes.
